content.content:
## General public / engaged citizens

**Trust in fact-checkers is deeply partisan.** Pew found 70% of Republicans say fact-checkers "tend to favor one side" vs 29% of Democrats — a 41-point gap; overall Americans split roughly 50/48 on whether fact-checkers deal fairly ([Pew Research, 2019](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2019/06/27/republicans-far-more-likely-than-democrats-to-say-fact-checkers-tend-to-favor-one-side/)). The academic literature confirms the audience skew: awareness, positive attitudes and self-reported use of fact-checking sites concentrate among liberals, mainstream-news consumers, and the more educated ([Robertson, Mourão & Thorson 2020, International Journal of Press/Politics](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/1940161219898055)); Republicans are more skeptical of all fact-check label types ([HKS Misinformation Review](https://misinforeview.hks.harvard.edu/article/journalistic-interventions-matter-understanding-how-americans-perceive-fact-checking-labels/)). Implication for a browse-anyone tool: neutrality of method does not buy a neutral audience.

**The backfire effect is largely debunked — corrections work.** Wood and Porter's replication attempts (5 experiments, 10,000+ participants, 52 issues) found no items triggering backfire ([ScienceDirect review](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2211368120300516)); Nyhan and co-authors now argue durability of misperceptions is not explained by backfire ([PNAS 2020](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1912440117)); Full Fact's own review reached the same conclusion ([Full Fact report, PDF](https://fullfact.org/media/uploads/backfire_report_fullfact.pdf)). Subjects even accept corrections of allied politicians, though belief improvements are modest.

**Demand is event-driven and spiky, not steady.** Google searches for "fact check" spiked +650% during a November 2019 Democratic debate ([The Hill](https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/471437-heres-what-searches-spiked-on-google-in-response-to-democrats-debate/)), and a broad debate fact-check was among the top queries during a 2024 VP debate ([Washington Examiner](https://www.washingtonexaminer.com/news/campaigns/presidential/3174106/what-people-were-searching-vp-debate/)). The same pattern shows on Wikipedia: candidate pageviews surge just before elections and correlate with outcomes ([EPJ Data Science](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1140/epjds/s13688-016-0083-3); [Washington Post on the mechanism](https://www.washingtonpost.com/graphics/politics/2016-election/presidential-wikipedias/)), with Nikki Haley's page reportedly reaching ~450K views/day around the 2024 early contests (traffic figures per search-result coverage; not independently verified). Baseline fact-check site traffic is modest between events — per Ahrefs, PolitiFact saw ~122K visits in May 2025 vs Snopes ~252K ([Ahrefs](https://ahrefs.com/websites/politifact.com/competitors); analytics-vendor estimate, not publisher-reported). Reuters Institute's 2025 report adds that when people verify suspicious content they go first to trusted news brands, but increasingly also to AI chatbots and social media — a "flatter" verification hierarchy ([DNR 2025 executive summary](https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/digital-news-report/2025/dnr-executive-summary)); 58% globally worry about telling real from fake news, 73% in the US ([full PDF](https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/sites/default/files/2025-06/Digital_News-Report_2025.pdf)).

## Journalists and fact-checkers

**The claim-finding step is already partially automated — by the fact-checking community itself.** Duke Reporters' Lab's Tech & Check runs ClaimBuster over transcripts and social posts and emails fact-checkers daily lists of checkable statements; its Fact-Check Insights database holds structured data on 180,000+ checked claims via the ClaimReview schema ([Duke Sanford](https://sanford.duke.edu/blog-post/duke-reporters-lab-gives-fact-checkers-researchers-new-tools-thwart-misinformation/)). This is the strongest signal of what the bottleneck is: finding and re-finding what a figure said, at scale, across sources.

**Their current tool stack is fragmented and expensive.** Broadcast monitoring runs through TVEyes (2.5M+ hours of broadcast/month, real-time transcripts and alerts — [TVEyes](https://www.tveyes.com/)) and clip marketplaces like Grabien, which monitors live events and sells professionally cut, transcribed clips ([Grabien](https://grabien.com/)). Print archive search means Nexis, historically ~$600/month per seat — a freelancer-negotiated group deal at $26/month was newsworthy in itself ([Tools for Reporters](https://toolsforreporters.com/2021/03/24/a-nexis-for-the-rest-of-us/)). Transcription is commodity, with the key journalist feature being timestamp-linked audio for quote verification ([The Media Copilot](https://mediacopilot.ai/the-best-ai-transcription-tools-for-journalists-hands-on-review/)). C-SPAN's archive — 200,000+ hours since 1987, word-level searchable — is the free gold standard but covers only official proceedings and its own programming ([Purdue researcher guide, PDF](https://cla.purdue.edu/communication/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/How-To-Guide-for-Researchers-C-SPAN-Archives.pdf)).

**The people doing this work are disappearing.** 270,000+ US newspaper jobs gone since 2005 (75%+); 1,200 newspaper and 1,800 digital-publisher journalist jobs lost in the past year alone ([Medill State of Local News 2025](https://localnewsinitiative.northwestern.edu/projects/state-of-local-news/2025/report/); [Nieman Lab](https://www.niemanlab.org/2025/10/in-medills-latest-state-of-local-news-report-a-festering-20-year-old-problem-looms-larger-than-ever/)). Full-time newspaper statehouse reporters fell from 374 (2014) to 245 (2022) ([Pew media layoffs topic page](https://www.pewresearch.org/topic/news-habits-media/news-media-trends/media-industry/media-layoffs-employment/)). Fact-checking itself is contracting: Duke's census counted 443 active projects in 2025, down from 451, with ~30 closures vs 10 launches, as Meta ended its US third-party program ([Duke census — reporterslab.org is egress-blocked from this environment; figures per search results attributing them to the Duke Reporters' Lab censuses](https://reporterslab.org/2025/06/19/fact-checkers-persevere-as-politicians-platforms-turn-up-heat/); see also [Poynter on the 2026 census](https://www.poynter.org/fact-checking/2026/fact-checking-projects-survive-funding-cuts-duke-census/)). IFCN's State of the Fact-Checkers surveys report 76% of organizations describing finances as vulnerable or in crisis even while 62% grew audiences, and ~72% facing harassment ([Rappler on the 2025 report](https://www.rappler.com/world/global-affairs/state-fact-checkers-report-2025-ifcn/); [Poynter on the 2023 report](https://www.poynter.org/ifcn/2024/state-fact-checkers-report-2023-findings/)). A CHI 2025 study documents fact-checkers' explicit requirement that any automated assistance show its evidence trail — opaque verdicts are unusable to them ([ACM CHI 2025](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3706598.3713277)).

## Researchers and academics

The academic literature confirms the audience skew: awareness, positive attitudes and self-reported use of fact-checking sites concentrate among liberals, mainstream-news consumers, and the more educated ([Robertson, Mourão & Thorson 2020, International Journal of Press/Politics](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/1940161219898055)); Republicans are more skeptical of all fact-check label types ([HKS Misinformation Review](https://misinforeview.hks.harvard.edu/article/journalistic-interventions-matter-understanding-how-americans-perceive-fact-checking-labels/)). Implication for a browse-anyone tool: neutrality of method does not buy a neutral audience.

**The backfire effect is largely debunked — corrections work.** Wood and Porter's replication attempts (5 experiments, 10,000+ participants, 52 issues) found no items triggering backfire ([ScienceDirect review](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2211368120300516)); Nyhan and co-authors now argue durability of misperceptions is not explained by backfire ([PNAS 2020](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1912440117)); Full Fact's own review reached the same conclusion ([Full Fact report, PDF](https://fullfact.org/media/uploads/backfire_report_fullfact.pdf)). Subjects even accept corrections of allied politicians, though belief improvements are modest.

**Demand is event-driven and spiky, not steady.** Google searches for "fact check" spiked +650% during a November 2019 Democratic debate ([The Hill](https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/471437-heres-what-searches-spiked-on-google-in-response-to-democrats-debate/)), and a broad debate fact-check was among the top queries during a 2024 VP debate ([Washington Examiner](https://www.washingtonexaminer.com/news/campaigns/presidential/3174106/what-people-were-searching-vp-debate/)). The same pattern shows on Wikipedia: candidate pageviews surge just before elections and correlate with outcomes ([EPJ Data Science](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1140/epjds/s13688-016-0083-3); [Washington Post on the mechanism](https://www.washingtonpost.com/graphics/politics/2016-election/presidential-wikipedias/)), with Nikki Haley's page reportedly reaching ~450K views/day around the 2024 early contests (traffic figures per search-result coverage; not independently verified). Baseline fact-check site traffic is modest between events — per Ahrefs, PolitiFact saw ~122K visits in May 2025 vs Snopes ~252K ([Ahrefs](https://ahrefs.com/websites/politifact.com/competitors); analytics-vendor estimate, not publisher-reported). Reuters Institute's 2025 report adds that when people verify suspicious content they go first to trusted news brands, but increasingly also to AI chatbots and social media — a "flatter" verification hierarchy ([DNR 2025 executive summary](https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/digital-news-report/2025/dnr-executive-summary)); 58% globally worry about telling real from fake news, 73% in the US ([full PDF](https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/sites/default/files/2025-06/Digital_News-Report_2025.pdf)).

## Journalists and fact-checkers

**The claim-finding step is already partially automated — by the fact-checking community itself.** Duke Reporters' Lab's Tech & Check runs ClaimBuster over transcripts and social posts and emails fact-checkers daily lists of checkable statements; its Fact-Check Insights database holds structured data on 180,000+ checked claims via the ClaimReview schema ([Duke Sanford](https://sanford.duke.edu/blog-post/duke-reporters-lab-gives-fact-checkers-researchers-new-tools-thwart-misinformation/)). This is the strongest signal of what the bottleneck is: finding and re-finding what a figure said, at scale, across sources.

**Their current tool stack is fragmented and expensive.** Broadcast monitoring runs through TVEyes (2.5M+ hours of broadcast/month, real-time transcripts and alerts — [TVEyes](https://www.tveyes.com/)) and clip marketplaces like Grabien, which monitors live events and sells professionally cut, transcribed clips ([Grabien](https://grabien.com/)). Print archive search means Nexis, historically ~$600/month per seat — a freelancer-negotiated group deal at $26/month was newsworthy in itself ([Tools for Reporters](https://toolsforreporters.com/2021/03/24/a-nexis-for-the-rest-of-us/)). Transcription is commodity, with the key journalist feature being timestamp-linked audio for quote verification ([The Media Copilot](https://mediacopilot.ai/the-best-ai-transcription-tools-for-journalists-hands-on-review/)). C-SPAN's archive — 200,000+ hours since 1987, word-level searchable — is the free gold standard but covers only official proceedings and its own programming ([Purdue researcher guide, PDF](https://cla.purdue.edu/communication/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/How-To-Guide-for-Researchers-C-SPAN-Archives.pdf)).

**The people doing this work are disappearing.** 270,000+ US newspaper jobs gone since 2005 (75%+); 1,200 newspaper and 1,800 digital-publisher journalist jobs lost in the past year alone ([Medill State of Local News 2025](https://localnewsinitiative.northwestern.edu/projects/state-of-local-news/2025/report/); [Nieman Lab](https://www.niemanlab.org/2025/10/in-medills-latest-state-of-local-news-report-a-festering-20-year-old-problem-looms-larger-than-ever/)). Full-time newspaper statehouse reporters fell from 374 (2014) to 245 (2022) ([Pew media layoffs topic page](https://www.pewresearch.org/topic/news-habits-media/news-media-trends/media-industry/media-layoffs-employment/)). Fact-checking itself is contracting: Duke's census counted 443 active projects in 2025, down from 451, with ~30 closures vs 10 launches, as Meta ended its US third-party program ([Duke census — reporterslab.org is egress-blocked from this environment; figures per search results attributing them to the Duke Reporters' Lab censuses](https://reporterslab.org/2025/06/19/fact-checkers-persevere-as-politicians-platforms-turn-up-heat/); see also [Poynter on the 2026 census](https://www.poynter.org/fact-checking/2026/fact-checking-projects-survive-funding-cuts-duke-census/)). IFCN's State of the Fact-Checkers surveys report 76% of organizations describing finances as vulnerable or in crisis even while 62% grew audiences, and ~72% facing harassment ([Rappler on the 2025 report](https://www.rappler.com/world/global-affairs/state-fact-checkers-report-2025-ifcn/); [Poynter on the 2023 report](https://www.poynter.org/ifcn/2024/state-fact-checkers-report-2023-findings/)). A CHI 2025 study documents fact-checkers' explicit requirement that any automated assistance show its evidence trail — opaque verdicts are unusable to them ([ACM CHI 2025](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3706598.3713277)).

## Researchers and academics

## Who these segments actually are in Israel

The four segments below were researched against the US and are kept as transferable background on how people respond to corrections and what practitioners need. This section is the Israeli reading of the same four, and it is where the sizes and the habits come from.

**The public: online, messaged, and only half-trusting.** The Israel Democracy Institute's media survey (published 26 May 2024, led by Tehilla Shwartz Altshuler and Inna Orly Sapozhnikova) found 63% of respondents check news online daily, 59.5% use social media for news, 58% rely on television, **52% get news through WhatsApp or Telegram**, 36% radio and 16% print. Average trust in the media stood at 46%, split hard by outlet: Kan 11 at 60%, Channel 12 at 54%, Channel 13 at 46%, Channel 14 at 35%. 56% believe they can distinguish fake news from factual reporting, and about 70% believe they can separate news from commentary ([IDI: Media and Social Media Consumption, Trust, and Literacy](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/54235)). Two things follow. Messaging apps are a first-class news channel here in a way they are not in the US data above, so a shareable per-statement link matters more than a destination site. And the trust split runs by *channel*, not only by party — which is the Israeli form of the partisan-audience problem the US section describes.

**A fifth of the country is outside the survey and outside the language.** The IDI survey covered the Jewish population only; a companion survey of Arab citizens' habits was planned separately. Arab citizens are 2.147 million people, 21.1% of the population ([CBS figures as reported](https://israel.com/public/israel-starts-2026-with-more-than-10-million-people/)). A Hebrew-only product does not serve them, and the benchmark evidence about Israeli media habits does not describe them either — both gaps are real and neither is closed by more Hebrew research.

**Trust in the institutions being tracked is itself low.** IDI's Democracy Index 2025 — its 23rd — found trust in state institutions near record lows for a second year, with trust in the government at 25% among Jewish respondents and 17.5% among Arab respondents, though the general mood improved sharply (34% called the country's situation bad or very bad, down from 54%) ([IDI, Israeli Democracy Index 2025, selected findings](https://en.idi.org.il/publications/62717); [Times of Israel](https://www.timesofisrael.com/ahead-of-election-year-survey-finds-israelis-trust-in-democracy-remains-low/)). Separately, fewer than half the public expressed trust in the prime minister ([IDI, 40% overall](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/59940)). A statements corpus is a low-trust-environment product: the audience's default is suspicion of the figure *and* of whoever is reporting on the figure, which argues for showing sources over asserting verdicts.

**Journalists here are under pressure, not just under-resourced.** The US section's story is contraction. Israel's adds coercion: RSF's 2025 index placed Israel 112th of 180, down from 101st, and RSF documents a year of pressure, intimidation and censorship of Israeli journalists ([RSF](https://rsf.org/en/pressure-intimidation-and-censorship-israeli-journalists-have-faced-growing-repression-past-year)); CPJ reported in December 2025 on stepped-up censorship and suppression of independent reporting ([CPJ](https://cpj.org/2025/12/under-the-radar-israel-steps-up-censorship-and-suppression-of-independent-reporting/)); in November 2024 the cabinet voted to end all government advertising in and subscriptions to *Haaretz* ([Courthouse News](https://www.courthousenews.com/chilling-effect-israel-reforms-raise-press-freedom-fears/)). (These figures come from search-result reporting; rsf.org's own index and country pages returned HTTP 403 to this environment.) The practical implication for a tool: a journalist who will be attacked for a claim needs the receipt more than the verdict — the evidence trail that the CHI 2025 study found fact-checkers demand is not a nicety here.

**Professionally, the fact-checking "segment" is one desk.** HaMashrokit at *Globes* is Israel's only IFCN-accredited fact-checker (see the competitor wiki). Where the US segment is hundreds of organisations competing for the same funders, the Israeli one is a handful of people — so the realistic relationship is supply, not substitution: a corpus that makes their monitoring step cheaper.

**Researchers here are unusually well supplied — with parliamentary text.** The post-Twitter data vacuum the US section describes is real in Israel too for social and broadcast speech, but the parliamentary half is solved: the Knesset Corpus covers 1992–2024, 30M+ sentences, annotated and distributed through CLARIN's ParlaMint ([Language Resources and Evaluation](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10579-025-09833-4)), and Hebrew-specific models are trained on exactly it ([Knesset-DictaBERT](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.20581)). Israeli academic demand is therefore likelier to be for what the corpus *lacks* — studio interviews, rallies, party channels — than for the chamber record.

**Campaign and advocacy staff have a date.** The election is 27 October 2026 ([Times of Israel](https://www.timesofisrael.com/judge-sets-date-for-next-scheduled-elections-for-october-2026/)). Whether Israeli party apparatuses or campaign consultancies buy statement archives — and from whom — was not established this pass and is an open question below; the American Bridge-scale opposition-research industry described in the US section has no confirmed Israeli equivalent.

## Public fact-checkers

**PolitiFact** is the most direct precedent for inconsistency tracking. Its [Flip-O-Meter, introduced in 2008](https://www.politifact.com/article/2008/aug/05/introducing-flip-o-meter/), rates an official's *consistency* on an issue — No Flip / Half Flip / Full Flop — explicitly framed as not a value judgment about changing positions. It is still in active use: PolitiFact ran a [Full Flop on Trump's TikTok-ban reversal in January 2025](https://www.politifact.com/factchecks/2025/jan/16/donald-trump/flip-flop-trump-now-opposes-a-tiktok-ban-in-2020-h/), and maintains a [rolling list of Full Flop rulings](https://www.politifact.com/factchecks/list/?ruling=full-flop). The crucial limitation: it's editorial and case-by-case — a reporter writes each Flip-O-Meter item like a fact-check ([same process as the Truth-O-Meter](https://www.politifact.com/article/2013/may/31/principles-politifact/)); there is no continuously maintained per-figure statement corpus behind it. PolitiFact also runs promise trackers for the fourth presidency in a row — the [MAGA-Meter](https://www.politifact.com/article/2025/jan/19/politifact-donald-trump-2024-promises-maga-meter/) tracks ~75 second-term promises with Kept/Broken/Compromise/Stalled ratings.

## The Israeli field — who is already in this space

The four sections below survey the **US and UK** alternatives and are retained as precedent: how these products die (platform dependence, funder dependence), and what shapes have been tried. This section is the field the product actually competes in.

**knesset-ai.com — the closest live competitor, and nobody's name is on it.** [knesset-ai.com](https://knesset-ai.com/) describes itself as "one landing page for Knesset discussions, laws, votes, MK members and political undercurrents". It carries plenary and committee protocols from the last five years, every law passed in third reading, full voting maps, and **per-MK pages with ideological analysis, "surprising votes", and recent quotes from proceedings with links to the protocols the member's name appears in** — statement tracking from 2022-01-01 onward. Access appears free; no operating organisation, funder or team is identified on the page, and no pricing is stated. This is the single most important competitive finding of this pass: much of the corpus-plus-per-figure-browsing layer already exists in Hebrew. What could not be established is who runs it, whether it is maintained, how good the extraction is, and whether it does anything with contradictions — all open questions below.

**HaMashrokit (המשרוקית) of *Globes* — the verdict layer, with no corpus behind it.** Israel's only IFCN-accredited fact-checker, a signatory since 2018, operating as an independent unit inside *Globes* since January 2019 after two years (2017–2018) as an NGO; 300+ published checks since the July 2017 launch, roughly one item a day ([IFCN listing](https://ifcncodeofprinciples.poynter.org/application/public/the-whistle/661a8b0fba7689d48142c10b), [New Israel Fund on the *Globes* move](https://nif.org/stories/human-rights-democracy/the-whistle-integrated-into-globes-newspaper/)). Its published method is a five-stage pipeline — monitoring of radio, TV and social media by listeners; an editorial decision on whether a statement is checkable and publicly relevant; research against official sources and experts; editorial review including a right of reply; then a collective score — on a five-category scale: correct, inaccurate, misleading, false, and "לשיקולכם" ("for your judgment") for claims too complex to rate ([Globes, about HaMashrokit](https://www.globes.co.il/news/article.aspx?did=1001372882); the scale was reworked from ten categories to five in August 2025). Its [2025 year-in-review](https://www.globes.co.il/news/article.aspx?did=1001530848) reports that 57% of checked statements came out false or misleading, only 7% true-and-newsworthy (which the desk calls too low), and about an eighth nuanced or context-dependent; it names its own coverage gaps candidly — Arab parties, which appear little in Hebrew media, ultra-Orthodox parties, which speak through religious outlets, and Benny Gantz's State Camp.

The relationship to this product is complementary rather than competitive, and the shape of the gap is precise: HaMashrokit selects a claim, adjudicates it and publishes a verdict. It does not maintain a browsable per-figure record of what a figure has said over time, and its monitoring step — people listening to radio and TV — is exactly the step a corpus makes cheap. Its coverage gaps are also a corpus's natural strength: a chamber-record corpus captures Arab and Haredi MKs speaking in the Knesset regardless of whether they appear on Hebrew television.

**Ifat Group (קבוצת יפעת) — the incumbent, and it sells to institutions.** Israel's dominant media-monitoring company, tracking newspapers, radio, television and the internet since 1947, with transcription and translation alongside; thousands of items collected daily around the clock from every Israeli outlet, processed by both software and human media researchers and delivered to clients in real time ([Ifat](https://ifat.co.il/), [Hebrew Wikipedia](https://he.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D7%A7%D7%91%D7%95%D7%A6%D7%AA_%D7%99%D7%A4%D7%A2%D7%AA)). Its named competitors in online listening are Buzzilla and SpyTheNet. This is the Israeli analogue of the Meltwater/Cision layer described below, with the same structural gap: the output is private alerts and clippings for a paying institution, not a public per-figure history. Ifat also sells to government — it appears as a supplier in the state procurement system ([government contract listing](https://mr.gov.il/ilgstorefront/he/p/4000563752)) — which makes it a plausible acquirer or channel as much as a rival.

**Open Knesset / the Public Knowledge Workshop (הסדנא לידע ציבורי).** The veteran Israeli civic-tech nonprofit; [oknesset.org](https://oknesset.org/) republishes Knesset data updated daily, including committee sittings with protocols "in a convenient format with speaker divisions", under a CC-BY API, with the tooling public at [`hasadna/knesset-data`](https://github.com/hasadna/knesset-data) and [`knesset-data-python`](https://github.com/hasadna/knesset-data-python). It is the closest thing to prior art for the ingestion half of this product and should be read before writing a fetcher. Its current maintenance level was not established this pass — the same civic-tech funding fragility the US section documents applies here, and an open question below asks it directly.

**Shakuf, The Seventh Eye and HaMakom — the reader-funded independent bloc.** [The Seventh Eye](https://www.the7eye.org.il/about) is Israel's media watchdog, funded entirely by small public donations, whose editorial team won the Sokolov Prize in 2023; since 1 January 2021 it has been operated under a licensing agreement by the Shakuf association, having announced the union in September 2020, and in 2022 the independent outlet "The Hottest Place in Hell" merged in as well ([Hebrew Wikipedia](https://he.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D7%94%D7%A2%D7%99%D7%9F_%D7%94%D7%A9%D7%91%D7%99%D7%A2%D7%99%D7%AA)). [Shakuf](https://shakuf.co.il/) describes itself as Israel's largest independent outlet, funded solely by thousands of citizens with no advertising and no capital or foundation money, covering the Knesset's work among its beats. Notably, The Seventh Eye has publicly criticised HaMashrokit's fact-checks more than once ([one example](https://www.the7eye.org.il/454394)) — Israel's accountability field argues with itself in public, which is worth knowing before assuming any of it is a natural ally.

**FakeReporter (פייק ריפורטר).** Founded December 2020 by activists and researchers, a non-profit crowdsourced research project against propaganda, disinformation, hate speech and incitement online, run through the Civic Center for Digital Defense; its investigations of foreign influence networks targeting Israel have been published domestically and internationally ([FakeReporter](https://fakereporter.net/en/english/), [Hebrew Wikipedia](https://he.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D7%A4%D7%99%D7%99%D7%A7_%D7%A8%D7%99%D7%A4%D7%95%D7%A8%D7%98%D7%A8)). Adjacent, not overlapping: its subject is coordinated networks, not what a named politician said last year.

**The folk substitute.** Hebrew [Wikiquote](https://he.wikiquote.org/wiki/%D7%A1%D7%99%D7%A1%D7%9E%D7%90%D7%95%D7%AA_%D7%91%D7%A4%D7%95%D7%9C%D7%99%D7%98%D7%99%D7%A7%D7%94_%D7%94%D7%99%D7%A9%D7%A8%D7%90%D7%9C%D7%99%D7%AA) carries per-politician quote pages and a "slogans in Israeli politics" page; the rest of the demand is met by listicles in the mainstream press ([Makor Rishon's 75 sentences](https://www.makorrishon.co.il/news/607477/), [N12's 25 unforgettable political phrases](https://www.mako.co.il/news-elections-2013/articles/Article-371da1d09391c31004.htm)). Undated, unsourced to a primary record, and curated for memorability — the manual status quo, in Hebrew.

108:## Where a US statements corpus can lawfully come from
118:## US legal and ethical terrain
122:On scraping: [hiQ v. LinkedIn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HiQ_Labs_v._LinkedIn) established that scraping publicly accessible data does not violate the CFAA (no criminal exposure), but hiQ ultimately [lost on breach-of-contract grounds and settled with a permanent injunction plus $500,000](https://www.zwillgen.com/alternative-data/hiq-v-linkedin-wrapped-up-web-scraping-lessons-learned/) — the live risk for a statements scraper is terms-of-service and contract claims from platforms, not prosecution ([Farella Braun analysis](https://www.fbm.com/publications/what-recent-rulings-in-hiq-v-linkedin-and-other-cases-say-about-the-legality-of-data-scraping/)). Government sources carry none of that contractual exposure — but the 2026-08-23 pass corrected the earlier form of this claim, which named "C-SPAN-style proceedings" among them: C-SPAN's own terms bar automated copying outright, so its archive is not a government source for this purpose. The safe backbone is the government's own publishers, with the Congressional Record's non-verbatim caveat attached — see [Where a US statements corpus can lawfully come from](#where-a-us-statements-corpus-can-lawfully-come-from) above.

input.body:
Closes #88

## What was researched

The wikis were seeded with US-only research while the product is Israeli and Hebrew, so this pass researched the Israeli market across all three pages. The US material is kept — it carries real transferable lessons — but is now explicitly labelled as background, and every page's `## Key insights` header leads with Israeli findings.

## The strongest findings

**The Israeli corpus position is structurally better than the US one the wiki described.** Verified first-hand this pass:

- **Copyright Act 5768–2007 §6** puts *"דברי הכנסת"* — Knesset proceedings — outside copyright by statute, alongside laws and judicial decisions. Where the US read had to route around C-SPAN's terms of use, here the exemption names parliamentary proceedings explicitly, and uses the same phrase the Knesset's own document system uses as the type name for the published record.

Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.

Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.

# Merge to main

If the project's own `CLAUDE.md` names a merge-policy file, that file overrides the divergent
points below (merge method, CI gating). Don't go hunting for one it doesn't name.

1. Load `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request` in one `ToolSearch`.
2. No PR open for the branch? `create_pull_request` (base `main`), body ending `Closes #<issue>`.
3. If the PR has check runs, wait for them to pass. None — merge without waiting.
4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Don't pre-read
   mergeability; the call fails loudly.
5. Sync local `main`: `git checkout main && git pull origin main`.
6. Capture the conversation:
   `node .claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`
   (in the canon repo: `node packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`). Skip only if
   the repo doesn't declare `claudinite-growth`. A later merge in the same session runs it again.
7. Run the basics pack's
   [verify-in-production](../../../basics/skills/verify-in-production/SKILL.md) skill, unasked.
   This step is that skill's **only** trigger — it files against what the squash actually landed,
   which is why it runs here and not when the code was written or the PR opened. It decides
   whether this change needs a production check at all — most don't — and files the issue that
   comes back once the change is live. Never offer the owner to check later instead.

Don't re-read the issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge.
